messages.subject: stan_lmer getting stuck
parts:
I have a fairly large data set (190k observations) with multiple parameters / interactions and 3 crossed, unbalanced groups, each with 100 to 1000 members.  

I'm used to working with this data set (and those like it) in lme4, but I would prefer to predict over a distribution rather than just means / modes.  The outputs are actually a series of categories, but each has a defined value in the currency of interest, so I am using those values to model the output as continuous and the relationship of the predictors to it as Gaussian.

The model resolves swiftly in lme4: about 3 minutes.  This is no surprise: lme4 is fast.  The predictions from the lmer model make good sense: except that confidence intervals are tricky without bootstrapping.  If I am going to do lots of bootstrapping, I'd rather do MCMC and get better answers along with decent intervals.

The model also works in MCMCglmm.  It takes an hour and a half to take 13000 samples (3000 of which are burnin), but the package models it fairly well.  MCMCglmm does use a method of Gibbs sampling that may be well suited for this application.  (Its predict function is also a memory hog, but that's another issue).

Stan_lmer, on the other hand, seems befuddled when asked to model the same data, and set to "sampling." The code seems to compile correctly, and warmup begins, but the chains quickly freeze or hang at 25 instances, once in a while getting to 50 and sometimes never getting off 0. The sampling has to be killed manually, which in turn requires terminating the R session, and there are no apparent diagnostics left behind when I reboot the session.

I've tried switching among the built-in priors, without success. Past posts have emphasized that Stan can handle large numbers of parameters, provided the priors are good.  But rstan_arm discourages switching the default priors. Another option might be to use the findings of the lmer model to set up priors and starting values for stan_lmer, but it feels like the problem here may be more fundamental that that.  Meanfield VI does converge, although the predictions are, as I would expect, not very good. 

The coefficients, intercepts, and outputs are all close to zero. Scaling the continuous coefficients (using R's built-in function anyway) has not helped.  

I am attaching a script containing dummy data (with scaled continuous variables) that replicates the problem, along with scripts for lme4, MCMCglmm, and stan_lmer that show what I am talking about. I'd appreciate any insight.  

All this said, rstan_arm is terrific and I thank you all for the package.  

Jonathan

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: stan_lmer getting stuck
parts:
On Friday, January 22, 2016 at 8:57:03 PM UTC-5, Jonathan Judge wrote:
I've tried switching among the built-in priors, without success. Past posts have emphasized that Stan can handle large numbers of parameters, provided the priors are good.  But rstan_arm discourages switching the default priors. Another option might be to use the findings of the lmer model to set up priors and starting values for stan_lmer, but it feels like the problem here may be more fundamental that that.  Meanfield VI does converge, although the predictions are, as I would expect, not very good.

This is a misinterpretation that I think stems from the startup message

- Do not expect the default priors to remain the same in future rstanarm versions.
Thus, R scripts should specify priors explicitly, even if they are just the defaults.

That doesn't mean that you should use the default priors; it means if you are going to use the default priors you should specify them explicitly rather than omitting them from the stan_lmer() call. That way, your scripts should still work the way you expect them to in a future version of rstanarm which may change the default arguments for the priors. Or maybe it is because specifying the priors on the group-specific parameters is a bit difficult, although it is not too hard when your model only has group-specific intercepts. I would say that if you are not going to specify informative coefficients on the common coefficients, then you should call stan_lmer() with QR = TRUE, which should help you sample efficiently if you are doing MCMC and may be essential for the variational approximation to the posterior to be reasonable if you are doing meanfield.

Also, we don't recommend scaling predictors by the sample standard deviation because that makes it hard to get the posterior predictions right. Scaling by constants is okay, but shouldn't really be necessary if QR = TRUE is specified.

All that said, it is going to take a while for a model with 190,000 observations and thousands of parameters.

Ben
